rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2 and 3 - the authors installed drip kits and hand-dug wells on 10 pilot household farms in three kebeles, monitored yields and water productivity, and surveyed/interviewed 60 farmers. Q2: Section 3.4, Figures 9-10 - the introduced drip system (with hand-dug wells) increased yields by 56 to 120% for all crops except maize compared with non-intervention surface-irrigated farms. Q5: Section 3.4, Figure 10 - yield differences are reported per crop (potatoes, carrots, garlic, onions, cabbage, maize), with maize the exception to the gain. Q6: Sections 2 and 3.4 - the yield effect is reported across 10 intervention household farms spread over three kebeles of the Haramaya District, compared with 50 non-intervention farms. Q7: Sections 3.4, 3.5 and 4 - the authors state that the regular water supply from private hand-dug wells is what enabled regular, effective drip irrigation, and that financial and technical support, capacity building, maintenance skills and access to kits/markets are needed for the system to work and be sustained. Q8: Section 4 - authors state limitations: socio-economic and biophysical factors (soil types and depths, nutrients, landscape, rainfall) were not considered; Section 2 notes the comparison assumed fertilizer, seed and management were similar.
rows.notes: Tomato, named in the passage, is not among the crops for which yields were measured (potatoes, carrots, garlic, onions, cabbage, maize). The intervention bundled drip irrigation with private hand-dug wells, so the yield gain cannot be attributed to drip alone. Q3: farmers' interview responses mention improved yields (Section 3.5), but this is a general perception statement rather than a separate assessment of the yield effect, so not counted as triangulation. Q4: the text asserts more regular water and uniform distribution over about 65% of farmland but the method behind this figure is unclear; water applied was used only to compute water productivity. Q5 answered yes on the basis of per-crop results in Figure 10, although the text also says only potato is presented, which is contradictory; three kebeles were chosen for different climate/hydrology but yield results per kebele are not clearly given. Q9: the 56-120% figure is a range across crops, not a dispersion measure for any result; no SD, SE or CI reported. Small sample (10 pilot farms, one season).

notes: Full text available (figures and tables not reproduced). Study is a pilot intervention with 10 drip plus hand-dug well household farms versus 50 non-intervention farms in three kebeles, with yield monitoring plus surveys and focus groups; one cropping season of yield data.
